questions.question: A medical diagnostic test has a 95% sensitivity and 90% specificity. If a disease has a 1% prevalence in the population, what happens to the probability that a person who tests positive actually has the disease (Positive Predictive Value)?
options: It is extremely high (over 90%) because sensitivity is 95%.
It is relatively low (around 8.7%) due to the low base rate of the disease (Bayes Theorem).
It is exactly equal to the specificity (90%).
It cannot be calculated without knowing the sample size.
questions.explanation: By Bayes' Theorem, with a low prior (1%), false positives from the 99% healthy majority outnumber true positives, making the posterior probability ~8.7%.

questions.question: According to the Central Limit Theorem (CLT), which of the following statements is true regarding the sampling distribution of the sample mean?
options: The population itself must be normally distributed for CLT to hold.
The sampling distribution of the mean approaches a normal distribution as sample size n increases, regardless of the population distribution shape (given finite variance).
The standard deviation of the sample mean increases as sample size increases.
CLT applies only to discrete distributions like Poisson and Binomial.
questions.explanation: The CLT guarantees that for sufficiently large sample sizes, sample means are approximately normally distributed with standard error Ïƒ/âˆšn.

questions.question: In hypothesis testing, what is a Type I error (Î±) and how does it relate to p-values?
options: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis; occurs when p-value > 0.05.
Rejecting a true null hypothesis (false positive); we reject the null when the p-value is less than the significance level Î±.
Incorrectly calculating the standard error of the estimate.
The probability of correctly accepting an alternative hypothesis (statistical power).
questions.explanation: A Type I error is rejecting the null hypothesis when it is actually true (false positive rate Î±).

questions.question: Which layer of the OSI model is responsible for end-to-end reliability, segmentation, and flow control (e.g. TCP)?
options: Network Layer (Layer 3)
Transport Layer (Layer 4)
Data Link Layer (Layer 2)
Session Layer (Layer 5)
questions.explanation: The Transport layer (Layer 4) manages end-to-end communication, connection establishment (TCP 3-way handshake), and flow control.

questions.question: In an IPv4 network, what is the usable host capacity of a /24 subnet (CIDR notation)?
options: 256 usable hosts
254 usable hosts (excluding network and broadcast addresses)
128 usable hosts
512 usable hosts
questions.explanation: A /24 subnet has 2^(32-24) = 256 total IP addresses, minus the network address (.0) and broadcast address (.255), leaving 254 usable host addresses.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP)?
options: Translates domain names into IP addresses
Maps an IP address (Network layer) to a MAC address (Data Link layer) on a local subnet
Encrypts traffic between client and server via TLS
Automatically assigns dynamic IP addresses to client devices
questions.explanation: ARP maps an IPv4 address to its physical MAC hardware address for local frame delivery on an Ethernet network.

questions.question: What is the most effective primary defense against SQL Injection vulnerabilities in backend database queries?
options: Blacklisting dangerous characters like quotes and semicolons
Using parameterized queries (Prepared Statements) or ORM abstraction
Encoding URL parameters with base64
Enabling HTTPS encryption on the web server
questions.explanation: Parameterized queries separate SQL code from user-supplied data at the database parser level, making SQL injection impossible.

questions.question: Which HTTP header provides mitigation against Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) by restricting the sources of executable scripts?
options: Access-Control-Allow-Origin
Content-Security-Policy (CSP)
Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS)
X-Frame-Options
questions.explanation: Content-Security-Policy (CSP) allows server operators to restrict which domain origins are allowed to execute scripts, styles, and fetch requests.

questions.question: What security mechanism protects against Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)?
options: Anti-CSRF synchronizer tokens and SameSite cookie attributes
Hashing passwords with bcrypt
Setting the HTTP Authorization header to Basic Auth
Disabling browser caching with Cache-Control: no-store
questions.explanation: Cryptographic CSRF tokens and SameSite=Strict/Lax cookie attributes ensure that state-changing requests originate from authentic user sessions.

questions.question: What is the difference between JavaScript Promise.all() and Promise.allSettled()?
options: Promise.all() rejects immediately if any promise fails; Promise.allSettled() waits for all promises to resolve or reject.
Promise.all() runs sequentially while Promise.allSettled() runs concurrently.
Promise.allSettled() only works in Node.js environments.
There is no functional difference between the two.
questions.explanation: Promise.all short-circuits on the first rejection, whereas Promise.allSettled waits for all inputs to complete and returns status objects.

questions.question: In TypeScript, what is the key difference between an interface and a type alias?
options: Interfaces support declaration merging (open for extension); type aliases can represent unions, primitives, and mapped types.
Interfaces are transpiled into JavaScript runtime objects; type aliases are deleted.
Type aliases cannot be implemented by classes.
Interfaces cannot extend other interfaces.
questions.explanation: Interfaces can be augmented via declaration merging, whereas type aliases are aliases for any type composition including union and intersection types.

questions.question: How does JavaScript event loop prioritize Microtasks (e.g. Promise.then, queueMicrotask) relative to Macrotasks (e.g. setTimeout, setInterval)?
options: Macrotasks always execute before any microtasks in the queue.
The entire microtask queue is processed to completion immediately after each task and before rendering/next macrotask.
Microtasks and macrotasks alternate execution in a round-robin schedule.
Microtasks run on a separate background thread in the browser.
questions.explanation: The JavaScript engine drains the microtask queue completely before moving to the next macrotask or browser paint cycle.

questions.question: What is the primary benefit of multi-stage Docker builds?
options: Runs multiple containers inside a single pod.
Separates build tools and dependencies from the final lean runtime image, minimizing image size and attack surface.
Automatically pushes images to Docker Hub.
Enables multi-threading for Python interpreters.
questions.explanation: Multi-stage builds compile artifacts in a heavy build stage and copy only binary/runtime artifacts to the minimal final stage.

questions.question: What is the difference between Docker CMD and ENTRYPOINT instructions in a Dockerfile?
options: ENTRYPOINT defines the default executable; CMD provides default arguments that can be easily overridden at runtime via docker run.
CMD is executed at build time; ENTRYPOINT is executed at container start.
ENTRYPOINT is deprecated in Docker 20+ in favor of RUN.
There is no difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT.
questions.explanation: ENTRYPOINT specifies the immutable command to invoke, while CMD supplies default parameters that can be overridden by arguments passed to docker run.

questions.question: Which Linux kernel features provide process isolation and resource limitation for Docker containers?
options: Namespaces (for process/network/mount isolation) and cgroups (for CPU/memory resource limits)
Hypervisors and virtual memory swapping
SELinux exclusively without kernel virtualization
Systemd user units and cron triggers
questions.explanation: Containers are isolated via Linux Namespaces (PID, NET, MNT, IPC, UTS) and resource-constrained via Control Groups (cgroups).
